summary: This standards-track document gives guidelines for mail programs to send, deliver and display aggregate objects such as HTML pages that contain links to other parts. It was replaced by RFC 2557.

eli5.summary: An email carries a web page together with its pictures, so everything shows up properly when opened.

questions: send html with images in mime
how to send web pages in email
how to bundle images with html
subtitle: How to send web pages with pictures in email.

tldr.problem: Email messages can send HTML, but the images and resources the HTML references may not reach the recipient if they rely on downloading from the web. Network-dependent links may fail for offline recipients.
tldr.mechanism: MHTML bundles the HTML document with all its linked resources (images, stylesheets) into a single MIME message using multipart/related, and defines headers to map links to the bundled parts.
tldr.outcome: Recipients see the complete HTML page with images and styling, whether or not they have internet connectivity. RFC 2110 was replaced by RFC 2557, which made the same concept more precise.

today: RFC 2110 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 2557, which clarifies and refines the same concept. Both documents describe MHTML.

sections.title: Sending Aggregate Web Documents
sections.content:
HTML documents often reference other resources through links: images in <IMG> tags, stylesheets, applets, and frames. When sending such a document via email, the recipient needs not just the HTML markup, but all those linked resources as well. The RFC defines how to package them together in a single MIME message.

An alternative is to send only the URL and let recipients fetch the document themselves via HTTP, but that requires internet connectivity and assumes the recipient has access to the same resources. For offline recipients, corporate firewalls, or private internal web spaces, bundling everything in the email is essential.
sections.eli5: A web page is like a book with footnotes referring to other documents. Emailing just the book doesn't help unless the other person can look up those footnotes themselves.

sections.title: MIME Content Headers
sections.content:
Two new MIME headers help recipients map links in the HTML to the bundled resources. The Content-Location header specifies the URI that corresponds to a particular body part. The Content-Base header provides a base URI for resolving relative links within the HTML.

For example, if an HTML part references <IMG SRC="images/logo.gif">, a bundled image part can declare Content-Location: images/logo.gif. When the recipient's browser renders the HTML, it resolves relative links using Content-Base and matches them against the Content-Location headers of the other parts.
sections.eli5: The headers are address labels: one says what picture this is, the other says where to look for relative addresses, so the browser can find each picture when the page is displayed.

sections.title: Multipart/related Structure
sections.content:
When sending an aggregate document, the entire message uses the multipart/related MIME type. This content type groups the HTML document (the root part) with all its linked resources. Each resource becomes a separate body part with its own headers, including Content-Type and Content-Location.

The root part—typically the HTML document—should be indicated via a start parameter if it is not the first body part. Tools reading the message know to render the start part and use the other parts to resolve its links. This structure lets the sender avoid modifying the HTML itself: the original links remain unchanged, and the message structure handles the mapping.
sections.eli5: The whole email is wrapped as a package with sections: a main section for the HTML page, and extra sections holding each picture, so they're all together.

sections.title: Linking Strategies
sections.content:
The RFC describes two main strategies for linking bundled parts. The first uses Content-Location headers: each part declares its URI, and the recipient matches links in the HTML to those URIs. Relative URIs are resolved against Content-Base. This approach works with standard HTTP URIs and allows recipients to see where a resource came from or, if they have internet access later, fetch a fresher version from the same URI.

The second strategy uses CID (Content-ID) URLs and the cid: URL scheme. Instead of referencing a web URI, the HTML links directly to parts by their Content-ID (for example, <IMG SRC="cid:image123@example.com">). This makes the link unambiguous: it always refers to the bundled part, regardless of whether a resource with the same URI exists on the web.
sections.eli5: You can either label each picture with its web address, or give it a special in-the-email address so the browser knows exactly which bundled picture to show.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content:
Mailing a bundled document bypasses some network checks. The recipient sees cached copies of resources without verifying them against the live web versions. If an email claims an image is from a particular URI via Content-Location, there is no guarantee the actual resource at that URI is identical. Recipients should not cache such email-bundled resources in the same way they cache HTTP responses.

HTML documents can now be sent with executable content (JavaScript, Java applets), which email systems historically did not allow. Recipients must treat embedded scripts with the same caution as web content. Additionally, HTML documents may contain sensitive information (passwords, access tokens) in hidden fields or URLs, which users might inadvertently share if they forward an email-bundled page.
sections.eli5: Email-bundled web pages can hide the same tricks that web pages can, so be careful opening them from people you don't trust, just as you would on the web.
